report.source_text: Laboratory tests were remarkable for acute on chronic kidney injury (serum creatinine 3.63 mg/dL, baseline 2.93 mg/dL) (normal range 0.6–1.2 mg/dL) and hyperglycaemia 597 mg/dL (normal range 70–99 mg/dL). Thyroid stimulating hormone was 2.6 (normal range 0.4–4.2 mcU/mL). Venous blood gas showed pH 7.34, serum bicarbonate was 21 mmol/L (normal range 22–29). Urinalysis showed no ketosis. Calculated serum osmolarity was 308 mosm/kg (normal 280–305 mosm/kg) making hyperosmolar hyperglycaemia state unlikely. Hb A1c level returned elevated at 17.0% (normal <6.0%).

report.source_text: The patient was admitted to the hospital for further management. Intravenous hydration and subcutaneous basal and prandial insulin were administered. Serum blood glucose levels normalised over the next 24–48 hours. Severe hemichorea-hemiballismus persisted, which impaired his ambulation and sleep. Due to severe insomnia and overnight agitation, the patient was initially treated with escalating doses of olanzapine. Low-dose clonazepam was added to the regimen on day 3 hospitalisation with minimal improvement. On day 4 olanzapine was stopped and risperidone 2 mg nightly was started with improvement in both sleep and right arm and right leg chorea-hemiballismus. The patient’s clinical symptoms of hemichorea-hemiballismus were markedly improved prior to discharge on hospital day 6.

clinician.trajectory_summary: An elderly man with uncontrolled diabetes presented with sudden right-sided hemichorea and flinging movements. Initial brain imaging (CT and MRI) revealed left basal ganglia abnormalities—faint hyperdensity on CT and increased T1 signal intensity on MRI in the left putamen, lentiform, and caudate nuclei—without evidence of stroke. Laboratory tests on admission showed severe hyperglycemia (glucose 597 mg/dL), elevated HbA1c (17%), absence of ketosis, and near-normal serum bicarbonate and pH. The patient was treated with IV hydration, insulin, olanzapine, clonazepam, then risperidone, with marked symptomatic improvement of hemichorea by hospital day 6. There was no subsequent imaging to assess radiological evolution documented.
